title: Product Spotlight: FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 Keep Pace as Data Center Bandwidth Doubles
body_markdown:
Image


An AI cluster can only work as fast as the links between its processors. When those links fall behind, some of the most expensive hardware in the data center sits waiting for data.


So the industry is doubling link speeds again. According to[Dell’Oro Group](https://www.delloro.com/news/ai-back-end-switch-sales-to-approach-1-trillion-over-the-next-five-years/) , 1.6 Tbps ports in AI back-end switches are expected to ramp at least five times faster than 800 Gbps, driven by adoption across scale-up, scale-out and scale-across networks. This bandwidth is critical to maximizing utilization of expensive xPU resources. Inside the server, PCI Express® (PCIe®) 7 doubles the data rate between CPUs, xPUs, memory, storage and smart network interface cards ([SmartNICs](https://www.sitime.com/company/newsroom/blog/what-smartnic) ).


Every one of those links takes its timing from a clock on the board. Each doubling of bandwidth leaves that clock less room for error.


Today we are introducing FemtoClock™ 4 and VersaClock® 8, two clock families built for these faster links. FemtoClock 4 clocks the Ethernet switches that connect AI systems. VersaClock 8 clocks the PCIe links inside them. If you design either kind of board, this post covers what each device does and where it fits.


## Why Faster Links Need Cleaner Clocks


Each end of a high-speed link uses a serializer-deserializer (SerDes) to send and capture bits at precise intervals. The SerDes derives those intervals from a reference clock, commonly 156.25 MHz or 312.5 MHz for Ethernet.


No clock is perfect. Its edges arrive a little early or a little late, and that variation is called jitter. For clocks like these, it is measured in femtoseconds, or quadrillionths of a second. Jitter on the reference clock uses up part of the link’s timing margin.


That margin shrinks with every generation. For Ethernet SerDes, the typical limit on reference clock jitter fell from under 150 fs at 56G to under 90 fs at 112G and under 35 fs at 224G.


When a clock consumes too much of that margin, the link encounters more bit errors, and the maximum throughput is reduced. In this case, the target peak bandwidth cannot be attained.


## FemtoClock 4: Fewer Devices in the Switch Clock Tree


Network speeds have moved from 400 Gbps to 800 Gbps and are now moving to 1.6 Tbps, with 3.2 Tbps on the horizon. Each step raises lane speed, lane count or both. For the switch designer, that means tighter jitter limits, more clocks and more frequency domains to manage. The clock count shows the strain. Top-of-rack switches generally need more than 40 clocks, and the number is growing. Building that clock tree from many small devices takes board space and complicates routing.


FemtoClock 4 is a jitter attenuator and clock generator for top-of-rack and spine switches built on 224G SerDes. It sits beside the Ethernet switch ASIC and supplies its low-jitter SerDes clocks. One device drives up to 18 outputs across as many as six frequency domains.


Key features include:


- **Low phase jitter:** 19 fs RMS at 312.5 MHz in clock generator mode (12 kHz to 20 MHz, 4 MHz high-pass filter), which preserves timing margin on 224G SerDes links.
- **Multiple domains:** Up to six frequency domains across 18 outputs, for boards that need several clock frequencies.
- **Fewer devices:** Up to 18 outputs from one device reduce the part count in top-of-rack switches, which generally need more than 40 clocks.
- **Two package options:** 18 outputs in a 10x10 mm BGA or 12 outputs in a 9x9 mm BGA, so you can match the part to the design.


Image


## VersaClock 8: PCIe 7 Clocks for Dense Compute Boards


On the compute side, reference clocks serve two domains: PCIe interconnections and high-speed SerDes interfaces among CPUs, xPUs, memory, storage and SmartNICs. The step up from PCIe 6 to PCIe 7 doubles the data rate and tightens the reference clock jitter limit from 100 fs to 67 fs. The boards are also dense and run hot, so a clock device has to meet that limit while saving board space and keeping self-heating low.


VersaClock 8 is a programmable, all-in-one clock generator for these boards. One device supplies both PCIe 7 and high-speed SerDes reference clocks for CPUs, xPUs, memory and storage.


Key features include:


- **PCIe 7 jitter:** About 10 fs reference clock jitter for PCIe 7, which leaves margin for the rest of the link.
- **Low phase jitter:** 30 fs RMS at 312.5 MHz (12 kHz to 20 MHz, 4 MHz high-pass filter), which preserves timing margin on high-speed links.
- **Low power, high temperature:** Low power limits self-heating, and the device operates at up to 105°C, which suits hot, dense boards.
- **Small packages:** 5-, 9- and 12-output variants in QFN packages from 4x4 mm to 6x6 mm, so you can match the part to the board.
- **Smaller footprint:** The 12-output variant is about 40% smaller than a comparable solution, which frees board space.


Image


## The Bigger Picture


These two families can share a board. In a top-of-rack switch, FemtoClock 4 supplies the SerDes clocks while VersaClock 8 supplies the CPU and PCIe clocks.


Neither is a new name. FemtoClock and VersaClock have a 20-year heritage across multiple generations. If you have designed with them before, you know the architectures and can reuse existing software.


They are part of our Precision Timing portfolio, which spans oscillators, clocks, resonators and software.


FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 are in production and available now.
